title: Who made it, and what does it show?

---
order: 2
unit: origin
title: Who made it, and what does it show?
node: AC9HH7S03 n1
assumes: [AC9HH7S02 n1, AC9HS6S04 n1]
summary: "Two questions start every look at a source. Origin asks who made it, when and where. Content asks what it shows or says. They are different questions, and mixing them up is the most common mistake: a clay warrior shows a soldier, but that does not make a soldier its maker. Keeping origin and content apart is what lets the later questions, context and purpose, work."
language: maths
hook: "A clay warrior stands in a tomb in China. It is dressed as a soldier. So was it made by a soldier? Let's look at what the figure tells us, and what it doesn't."
---
Every source has two things you can ask about straight away.

**Origin** is where the source came from: **who** made it, **when** and **where**.

**Content** is what is in the source: **what** it shows, says or records.

They sound close, but they are different questions. A source can show one thing and have been made by someone quite different.

> **Source A: a clay warrior.** A life-size figure made of baked clay, standing about 1.8 metres tall. It is dressed as a soldier, with armour and a belt, and each figure has a different face. It was one of thousands buried near the tomb of the First Emperor of Qin, in what is now Shaanxi province, China. It was made by craftsmen in Qin workshops during the First Emperor's reign. Making the figures took many years, before the emperor died in 210 BCE.

## Predict: which question?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students can tell origin and content questions apart before they use them."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Which of these asks about a source's origin?"
  options: ["Who made it, and when?", "What does it show?", "Why do we care about it?", "How big is it?"]
  actual: "Who made it, and when. Origin is who, when and where. What it shows is content."
```

## Try: origin or content?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting facts about one source makes the difference visible: origin is about the maker and the time, content is about what is in it."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Each fact is about Source A, the clay warrior. Is it about its origin or its content?"
  options: ["Origin", "Content"]
  items:
    - ["It was made by craftsmen", "Origin", "That says who made it."]
    - ["It shows a soldier in armour", "Content", "That is what the figure looks like."]
    - ["It was made during the First Emperor's reign, before 210 BCE", "Origin", "That says when it was made."]
    - ["Each figure has a different face", "Content", "That is what you can see in it."]
    - ["It was made in Qin workshops", "Origin", "That says where it was made."]
    - ["Some figures carried real bronze weapons", "Content", "That is something it contains."]
```

Was your guess right? Origin is about the maker, and when and where it was made. Content is about what is in the source.

One thing to watch: where a source was **found** is not always where it was **made**. The warriors were found in pits near the emperor's tomb, in what is now Shaanxi province. Historians record that too, but it is the findspot, not the origin.

Now find the same things on the card itself. Watch for the sentence about where the figures were found.

The soldier's armour and the different faces are content. The pits near the tomb are where the figures were found, not where they were made." }

> **Source B: a bamboo slip.** A thin strip of bamboo with writing in ink. Many strips were tied together to make a page. These ones were buried with a Qin official in 217 BCE in a tomb at Shuihudi, in what is now Hubei province. They were written by officials of the Qin government. They list laws and rules, including rules for looking after grain stores and the punishments for people who break the rules.

### Ask the questions

Look at Source B. **Who** made it? Officials of the Qin government. **When**? Before 217 BCE, because that is when they were buried. **Where**? Somewhere in Qin territory. That is its origin. The tomb at Shuihudi is where the slips were **found**, which is useful to know but is not the same thing. **What** is in it? Rules for grain stores, and punishments. That is its content.

### Find Nib's mistake

Nib is a made-up student for this lesson. Look at Source A, the clay warrior.

## Vary: more sources

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Each task changes the case: origin of a new source, content of a new source, and a source with a tricky label."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Source C is a stone inscription the First Emperor had set up on a mountain around 219 BCE. It says he brought peace and one set of laws and measures to all. What is its origin?"
      options: ["Made for the First Emperor, around 219 BCE, on a mountain", "It tells of peace and one set of laws and measures", "Made by the emperor's enemies, after he died", "It praises the emperor for uniting the land"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That is what it says. That is content, not origin.", "Nothing on the card says that. It was set up by order of the emperor, around 219 BCE.", "That is what it says about him. That is content, not origin."]
      explain: "Origin is made for the First Emperor, around 219 BCE, on a mountain. What it says is its content."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which of these is about Source C's content?"
      options: ["It says the emperor brought peace and one set of laws", "It was set up around 219 BCE, on a tour", "It was set up on a mountain in Qin lands", "It was made by order of the First Emperor"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That says when it was made, which is origin.", "That says where it was set up, which is origin.", "That says who had it made, which is origin."]
      explain: "What the inscription says is its content. The others are about its origin."
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Source D is a museum label written in 2019 about the clay warriors. Is each fact about its origin or content?"
      options: ["Origin", "Content"]
      items:
        - ["It was written in 2019", "Origin", "That says when."]
        - ["It says each warrior was shaped in parts and then fitted together", "Content", "That is what it says."]
        - ["It was written by museum staff", "Origin", "That says who made it."]
        - ["It says the warriors were found by farmers in 1974", "Content", "That is something it reports."]
```

> **Source C: an inscription.** Words cut into stone, set up on a mountain by order of the First Emperor on one of his tours, around 219 BCE. It praises the emperor as a ruler without equal. It says he brought peace and order, that everyone now lives in peace, and that everyone lives under one set of laws, weights and measures.

> **Source D: a museum label (made up for this lesson).** A short text on a card next to a clay warrior in a museum, written in 2019 by museum staff. It says each warrior was shaped in parts and fitted together, and that farmers digging a well found the first figures in 1974.

## Practise: both questions together

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Using both questions together on new sources until asking them separately feels natural."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is each question about a source's origin or its content?"
      options: ["Origin", "Content"]
      items:
        - ["Who made it?", "Origin", "That asks about the maker."]
        - ["What does it show or say?", "Content", "That asks what is in it."]
        - ["When was it made?", "Origin", "That asks about the time."]
        - ["What can you see in it?", "Content", "That asks what is in it."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Dev says: 'The inscription praises the emperor, so the emperor wrote it.' What is the best reply?"
      options: ["What it says is content. Who wrote it is a separate question", "That is right: people do not usually praise someone else", "No: it praises him, so his enemies must have written it", "No: it praises him, so it is false, and we cannot know the maker"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Something can praise a person without being written by them. Rulers often had others make things for them.", "That still reads the maker off the content, just the other way round.", "Praise does not make it false, and it is a different question from who made it."]
      explain: "What the inscription says is its content. Who wrote it, and who had it made, is its origin."
```

```step

insight: "Writing origin and content separately for a source you choose makes the two questions yours."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I picked a source (from our unit, or one of Sources A to D) and wrote its origin (who, when, where) and its content (what it shows or says) on two separate lines. A partner read it and gave feedback on whether the two were kept apart." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: a source from another society

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "The same two questions work on a source from any society, so the skill moves with the student."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Source E is a silver coin made in the Roman empire. It shows an emperor's head, with words around the edge. It was struck in Rome around 100 CE. Is each fact about its origin or its content?"
  options: ["Origin", "Content"]
  items:
    - ["It was struck in Rome", "Origin", "That says where it was made."]
    - ["It shows an emperor's head", "Content", "That is what it shows."]
    - ["It was made around 100 CE", "Origin", "That says when."]
    - ["It has words around the edge", "Content", "That is what is on it."]
```

## Wider: when the origin is unclear

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Sometimes the origin is not known. That is itself something to say about a source."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I talked with a partner about a source where we do not know who made it or when (for example a small clay figure found with no record of where), and what we can still say about it." }
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: tell a source's origin (who made it, when and where) apart from its
  content (what it shows or says)
summary: "Students learn the first two questions to ask of any source: origin
  (who made it, when and where) and content (what it shows or says). The first
  of two hinge lessons on this skill: students who read the maker off the
  content (a soldier made it because it shows a soldier) carry the mistake into
  every later question about context and purpose."
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 6 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can say who made a source, when and where.
  - I can say what a source shows or says, without mixing that up with who made
    it.
  - I can keep origin and content apart in my own words.
struggle: Students answer 'who made it?' by looking at what the source shows. A
  clay soldier must have been made by a soldier. Ask 'Who might have made it?
  How do you know?' and let them argue before you settle it.
before: >
  This is a hinge lesson. Lesson 3 (context and purpose) only works if students
  can keep origin and content apart. If this lesson goes thinly, the later
  questions will be answered from the content alone. Spend the time here.


  The worked example is ancient China in the Qin and Han period. It is a model:
  for your own depth study, swap in sources from Egypt, Greece, Rome, India or
  another, with the same two questions. A silver Roman coin (Source E, typical)
  shows how one is swapped in.


  The source cards are plain-words descriptions, not quotations. The inscription
  (Source C) is the exception worth knowing: the original stones are mostly
  lost, and the words survive as copied in Sima Qian's history. The card
  summarises what the inscriptions are known to say, in our own words. The clay
  warriors and the bamboo slips from Shuihudi (1975) are real; the museum label
  (Source D) is made up. Dates: the figures and their weapons were made over
  many years of the First Emperor's reign (some bronze weapons carry dates from
  the 240s and 230s BCE, before unification in 221 BCE), so the card says
  'during his reign' rather than 'around 210 BCE'. Where the figures were made
  is stated only as 'Qin workshops' (historians think the workshops were near
  the capital and the tomb site); Shaanxi is given as where they were found, to
  keep made and found apart. Nib and Dev are made up.


  The first lesson (optional) covers primary and secondary. A class that has not
  done it can still use this lesson, though they will not yet have met the words
  primary and secondary.
running:
  - "Predict: ask for votes. 'Who made it?' and 'What does it show?' sound alike
    on purpose."
  - "Try: after the sort, stop at the note on findspots. Where the warriors were
    found (pits near the tomb) is not where they were made. Origin is who made
    it, when and where it was made."
  - "Label the card (board): the same ideas on the card's own sentences, with a
    third label for where it was found. Students who label the pits sentence as
    origin have mixed findspot and origin; send them back to the note. The board
    only checks the labels we planted."
  - "Worked example: let Nib's mistake sit before explaining it. Ask which line
    is wrong, then why."
  - "Vary: ask students to give the reason as well as the answer."
  - "Make: read one or two out if students are happy to, without names."
stuck:
  - see: A student says a soldier made the clay warrior because it shows a soldier.
    ask: Does what it shows tell you who made it?
    fix: Go back to the card. It was made by craftsmen in workshops. Showing a
      soldier is content.
  - see: A student says 'it is from China' is the whole origin.
    ask: Who made it? When? Which part of China?
    fix: Origin is who, when and where. Country alone is only one part of where.
  - see: A student puts a fact about the museum label into the wrong group.
    ask: Is that about how it was made, or what it says?
    fix: Go back to the label. When it was written and by whom is origin. What it
      says is content.
stretch: Some sources have no known maker. A small clay figure found with no
  record of where is hard to place. What can you still say about it? This is the
  same idea at greater width. It does not go on to the next lesson.
support: "A card with two columns: Origin (who, when, where) and Content (what
  it shows or says). Students write a fact in the right column before they
  sort."
leads: >
  Next in Source origin and purpose: Why was it made, and what was going on?
  (context and purpose).


  Wider (teacher choice, not part of the student steps): ACARA's elaboration for
  AC9HH7S03 includes "explaining the difficulties in identifying the origin and
  purpose of some sources, such as the Kimberley Bradshaw paintings". These are
  culturally significant to First Nations people and are not used as an example
  here. If you use them, start from ACARA's elaboration and ask your school's
  First Nations contact for community-approved material on how the Traditional
  Owners speak of them. Do not generalise from outside sources.
exit:
  q: A clay warrior shows a soldier in armour. What does that tell you about its
    origin, and what does it tell you about its content?
  a: "Nothing about its origin: who made it, when and where are separate
    questions. It tells you its content: what it shows."
explain: >
  **Origin** is who made a source, when and where. **Content** is what it shows
  or says.


  They are different questions. What a source shows does not tell you who made
  it.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: A clay warrior shows a soldier. Does that tell you who made it? What would
      you want to find out, and where might you look?
    prompts:
      - What does the figure show? What does it not show?
      - If a historian wanted to know who made it, what would help?
    notes: "Let students reach for 'a soldier'. Then ask what they would need to
      know to be sure. The pattern is the point: content does not answer
      origin."
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Two lists
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Show Source A. Ask half the class to write everything they can see
        (content) and half to write everything they would need to ask (origin).
        Compare the two lists.
      notes: The two lists should look different. If they overlap, ask which questions
        can be answered by looking.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Origin or content?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Read out facts about a source from your own unit. Students hold up one
        finger for origin and two for content.
      notes: Keep it quick. Stop on any fact that splits the room and ask for a
        reason.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which is origin?
      type: question
      q: Which of these is about a source's origin?
      options:
        - It was made by craftsmen in workshops
        - It shows a soldier in armour
        - Each figure has a different face
        - Some figures carried bronze weapons
      answer: 0
      explain: Who made it is origin. The others say what it shows.
```
